texto: Its body is about the size of a grain of rice.
But its legs can be five or six times longer than its body,
with thin dark bands at every knee.
Now look at that web. It is a tangled, three dimensional mess.
No neat spiral, no pattern,
just threads going everywhere. It looks abandoned. It is not.
That chaos is the trick.
A mosquito flying into the corner hits several threads at once, from different angles,
and gets tangled. And when another spider walks into it,
every step shakes the threads.
The cellar spider cannot see very well. It hunts by touch,
feeling those vibrations through its long legs.
So that ugly web is really an alarm system. And the spider hangs upside down
in the middle of it, all day long, waiting.
Most of its hunting happens at night, while you are asleep.
So how does a spider this fragile beat a black widow?
On paper, it should lose.
A black widow is heavier, its venom is much stronger, and its bite can
send a person to the hospital. But the cellar spider has one huge advantage.
Reach. Those long legs let it fight
from a distance, where the widow cannot touch it.
When the widow stumbles into the tangle, the cellar spider does not rush in.
It stays back, and it uses its long back legs to fling silk at its enemy,
strand after strand. It keeps wrapping,
faster and faster, until the widow can barely move.
Only then does it step in, and deliver one careful bite.
Spider experts have watched cellar spiders kill black widows,
and house spiders much bigger than themselves.
That is why some of them actually recommend leaving cellar spiders alone in garages
and basements, right where widows like to hide.
And sometimes, the cellar spider does not wait for its enemy to come.
It walks right into another spider's web,
and gently plucks the threads. To the owner,
that vibration feels exactly like an insect that just got stuck.
So the owner comes running to grab its dinner.
And dinner is waiting for it.
Scientists call this aggressive mimicry. It is like a hunter using a duck call,
except the duck is a spider.
Of course, the cellar spider has enemies too.
So it has one of the strangest defenses of any spider.
When something big gets too close, like a bird, a bigger spider,
or your finger, it starts to shake.
It whirls its body around and around in the web, so fast that it turns into a blur.
For a predator, it becomes almost impossible to tell
where the spider actually is. That is why you sometimes see one
vibrating wildly when the vacuum gets close. It is not attacking you.
It is trying to disappear.
Now, about that rumor. Maybe you heard it on the playground.
Daddy longlegs are the most venomous spiders in the world,
but their fangs are too short to bite you. It is one of the most famous bug myths ever.
And it is wrong, twice.
First, there is no evidence that its venom is unusually strong, and it is
not dangerous to people. Second, its fangs are not too short.
In one famous television experiment, a host
let a cellar spider bite him on purpose. The result?
A tiny burning feeling that faded after a few seconds.
So yes, it can bite. It almost never does. And it is less painful than a mosquito.
And the harvestman, the other daddy longlegs,
has no venom at all. Cellar spiders are also surprisingly devoted parents.
Most spiders wrap their eggs in a silk sac and leave them behind.
A cellar spider mother carries her eggs in her mouth.
She holds the little bundle in her jaws for weeks, wrapped in just a few threads of silk.
When the babies hatch, they stay close to her in the web for a while, before they leave to
find corners of their own. And they are tough little survivors.
A cellar spider can go for months without a single meal.
If something grabs one of its legs, it can let that leg go and escape.
That is why you sometimes find one getting around on six or seven legs.
It is fine. And it can live for two or three years, quietly guarding the
same corner. This spider is also one of the great world travelers.
It probably came from the warm parts of Asia.
But for centuries, it has hitched rides with people, hidden in boxes, ships, and luggage.
Today it lives inside buildings on every continent except Antarctica.
It is one of the most widespread spiders on Earth, and almost all of them live with us.
Those old dusty cobwebs in the corners of old houses?
Many of them were built by cellar spiders. So why are there so many in your house?
Because a cellar spider only stays where there is food.
It eats mosquitoes, gnats, moths, flies, small beetles, and of course,
other spiders. If your basement is full of cellar spiders,
it means there are a lot of other bugs down there. And they are being eaten, every single night.
So think of them as free pest control, and a warning light at
the same time. But how do you know which spider you are looking at?
Here is the quick test. A cellar spider is pale, almost see through,
with a tiny body and legs that seem to go on forever.
It hangs high up, in corners and along the ceiling. A black widow is the opposite. A shiny black,
round body, shorter, thicker legs, and a red hourglass underneath.
It hides low and out of sight, under shelves, in woodpiles,
in old boxes, and around the garage door. Pale and high up, let it be.
Shiny black and low, keep your hands away.
That is also why bug spray can backfire. Spray does not choose.
It kills the hunters along with the pests. And the pests usually bounce back much faster than
the spiders that were eating them. So what should you do when you find one?
The easiest answer is nothing. Let it work. If you don't want it over your bed,
slide a cup over it, slip a piece of paper underneath, and move it to the basement or the garage.
If there are too many, vacuum the old webs,
seal the cracks around windows and doors, and dry out the damp rooms.
Fewer bugs means fewer cellar spiders. They will move on by themselves.
And if you ever find a black widow, do not touch it. Call a professional.
So the next time you see that pale spider hanging in the corner, look at it a little differently.
It is not a sign of a dirty house. It is a night guard with eight
long arms, watching over a corner you never look at. It eats the mosquitoes.
It fights the widows. And it has never wanted anything from you.
So put the broom down, and let it keep its job.
